meta.title: Who really said "Those who dance appear insane to those who cannot hear the music"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Nietzsche never wrote it. It’s an anonymous 19th-century saying, recorded from 1813 and called an “old proverb” by 1927.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Those who dance appear insane to those who cannot hear the music'?
meta.ogDescription: Nietzsche is the internet’s favorite credit, but there’s no source. The idea is an anonymous 19th-century proverb, not his line.

answer.label: Not Friedrich Nietzsche — a 19th-century proverb
answer.authorDates: Idea recorded from at least 1813 · called an “old proverb” by 1927
answer.sourceLine: There is no source for this line in any of Nietzsche’s works, and the earliest attribution to him is a 2003 Usenet post — more than a century after his death. The thought is a widespread 19th-century saying: the earliest documented version appears in Germaine de Staël’s De l’Allemagne (1813), and by 1927 The Times of London was already calling it an “old proverb.”

source.heading: An anonymous saying, not a Nietzsche line
source.excerpt: Those who dance appear insane to those who cannot hear the music.
trail: Wikiquote files the line under Misattributed to Nietzsche, giving the earliest appearance as Germaine de Staël’s On Germany (1813) and noting it was called an “old proverb” in 1927.
Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence Nietzsche wrote it and traced precursor expressions through 19th-century literature, concluding the origin is anonymous.
The comedian George Carlin printed a version — “Those who dance are considered insane by those who can’t hear the music” — in Brain Droppings (1997), and in a later book explicitly labeled it “Anon.”
A separate false credit to a poet named “Angela Monet” circulated after Megan Fox tattooed the phrase in 2010; no such poet exists.
source.excerptNote: The most-shared form — “And those who were seen dancing were thought to be insane by those who could not hear the music” — is a modern paraphrase of an old idea, not a sentence found in any Nietzsche text.
source.rightsNote: The exact wording is an anonymous saying with no identifiable single-author source, so no copyright status can be asserted. The earliest documented precursor — Germaine de Staël’s De l’Allemagne (1813) — is long in the public domain, but it is a different phrasing, not this line.

author.bio: The saying has no single author. Its earliest documented form appears in Germaine de Staël’s De l’Allemagne (1813), and variations recur throughout 19th-century sermons, letters and novels. By 1927 it was already treated as a common proverb — long before the internet began crediting it to Nietzsche.

misattribution.heading: Why Nietzsche gets the credit
misattribution.intro: This feel-good line is one of the internet’s most reliable false Nietzsche quotes. It fits his love of dance-and-music imagery, so it gets pinned on him — but it predates him and appears in none of his writing.

items.why: No source exists in Nietzsche’s works; the earliest link to his name is a 2003 Usenet post. Wikiquote lists it as Misattributed and Quote Investigator found no evidence he said it.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is a shared 19th-century saying — recorded by Germaine de Staël in 1813 and called an “old proverb” by 1927 — not a sentence written by Friedrich Nietzsche, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: An old idea with many voices
lead: The image is old and recurring: to an outside observer who cannot hear the music, dancers look like they have lost their minds. Germaine de Staël used it in 1813; Victorian sermons, letters and novels reworked it through the 1800s; Henri Bergson touched the same idea in his 1900 essay on laughter. By 1927 a London newspaper simply called it an “old proverb.”

Nietzsche did write vividly about dance as an emblem of vitality — “I would only believe in a god who could dance” comes from Thus Spoke Zarathustra. That genuine affinity is exactly why this anonymous saying migrated onto his name in the internet era, even though the sentence itself is not his.
context.pull: By 1927 it was already an “old proverb” — decades before anyone thought to credit Nietzsche.
